props.title: Even the Rain
props.initialSlug: Clash of Conscience, Clash of Worlds

sections.content: **Even the Rain** (2011) brilliantly interweaves colonial history with modern exploitation through its meta-narrative about filming Christopher Columbus in Bolivia. Director Icíar Bollaín crafts a masterwork that mirrors **Apocalypse Now** (1979) in its "film within a film" complexity, while echoing the social consciousness of **Battle of Algiers** (1966). When a Spanish film crew arrives to shoot a historical drama about Columbus's arrival in the Americas, they become entangled in the real-life Cochabamba Water Crisis of 2000, creating powerful parallels between past and present forms of colonialism.

sections.content: Gael García Bernal delivers a nuanced performance as Sebastián, the idealistic director whose artistic vision collides with reality when his indigenous lead actor Daniel (Juan Carlos Aduviri) becomes a leader in the water protests. This mirrors similar tensions in **Salvador** (1986) and The Year of Living Dangerously (1982), where journalists must choose between documenting injustice and intervening. Luis Tosar's cost-cutting producer Costa undergoes the film's most dramatic transformation, echoing the moral awakening seen in **Hotel Rwanda** (2004).

The film's technical achievement lies in its seamless integration of three narrative layers: the Columbus film being shot, the water protests, and the crew's personal journeys. This complexity recalls **8½** (1963) and **Day for Night** (1973), while its treatment of indigenous rights connects to films like Embrace of the Serpent (2015) and **Dance with Wolves** (1990). The water crisis footage feels documentary-real, reminiscent of **The Battle of Chile** (1975). SUBHEAD: Colonial Legacy and Modern Resistance

sections.content: What sets **Even the Rain** apart is its unflinching examination of how historical colonialism persists in modern economic systems. This theme connects to films like **Sugar** (2008) and **Sin Nombre** (2009), which explore exploitation in Latin America. The water privatization crisis becomes a perfect metaphor for resource extraction, echoing documentaries like **Flow: For Love of Water** (2008) and **Blue Gold: World Water Wars** (2008).
